paras: The attempted lynching of Sylvester Henderson took place in St. Louis, Missouri, on the evening of January 24, 1882, when a crowd put a rope around the neck of Henderson, an ash gatherer said to have fatally cut a man named Richard Hinch. Policemen took Henderson to the station before the crowd could hang him, and he survived. The episode reached print as a single brief wire item, which gave no one's race.

According to a National Press Association dispatch dated St. Louis, January 24, Henderson "fatally cut Richard Hinch this evening." The dispatch gave no cause for the cutting and no place within the city where it happened. Soon afterward, "the crowd put a rope around the neck of Henderson and were about to lynch him" when policemen arrived and "rushed him off to the station." The report named no members of the crowd and did not say how large it was.
No report of an inquest into Hinch's death, a charge against Henderson, a trial or arrests among the crowd appears in the coverage found.

The Omaha Daily Bee printed the dispatch on its front page on January 25 under the headline "A Bad Man," among other short telegraphic items. The wire stated Henderson's cutting of Hinch as fact rather than as an accusation, and it described the crowd's attempt without comment. It identified Henderson only by his work as an ash gatherer and named the race of no one involved, so the report does not show whether the episode was racial. No other paper's version, from St. Louis or elsewhere, was found.

chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A crowd put a rope around Henderson's neck and was "about to lynch him" before policemen took him away, an attempted lynching with no death (A1).

Henderson was not killed: policemen rushed him to the station after a crowd put a rope around his neck (A1). The attempt was extralegal and followed his alleged fatal cutting of Hinch, but no one died at the crowd's hands.
The only report found is one National Press Association wire item printed in the Omaha Daily Bee (A1).
